dialogues.speaker: Xingqiu
dialogues.text: "...Flurry of frost and autumn leaves. How they scatter! How they swirl."

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Heh, I knew you'd come today. I haven't been here long, actually. This must be exactly what they mean by great minds thinking alike and the understanding shared by kindred spirits!

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Did your brother end up reclaiming his book?

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: No, he hasn't. He did see me reading as I practiced my swordsmanship, and he did sigh, shake his head, and make gestures with his feet and hands... but he didn't ask for the book back.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: So, why did he suddenly...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Well... My guess is that this was my father's idea. He's always told me to practice my calligraphy more and pen a few more congratulatory notes on behalf of the family.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: That way, I could temper my mind, and also gradually get in touch with our business partners, which would lay a foundation for my future role in managing our family affairs.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: And besides, I don't know who else could open my brother's bookcase, if not my father...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: But you know me. I'm honestly most afraid of being stuck sitting up straight at a reception table, feigning civility and giving lip service to... Ahem! Sorry, pretend I never said that...

choices.text: Yeah, that sounds like it'd be really grating.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Right? *sigh* I'd much rather find a quiet spot to practice penmanship on my own than sit there drinking stale tea and listening to staler conversation...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: So, I came here under the pretext of working my swordsmanship into my calligraphy and gaining the relevant "enlightenment" from "Chronicle of Cleansing Ink." That way, I get to do a bit of both.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: I didn't expect that you'd show up so quickly, though. It seems that my swordplay was quite the effective signal beacon.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: And what enlightenment have you gained, perchance?

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: I've realized that even famous figures have an earnest side to them. They aren't prideful, haughty beings of divine skill, as many think.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: As you can see, this "original annotated copy" contains some remarks and critiques made by a who's-who of swordplay and calligraphy from a previous generation.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: One can, even if vaguely, glimpse the personalities of those eminent personages shining through. Take this, for example...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: This is another calligraphy great who didn't get along with Xifan. See how he nitpicks and hangs on to every little error, and how long his annotations are.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: See, this is the commentary he gave on Xifan's calligraphy: "Free, unrestrained, sharp as a bared edge, like a great tree braced against the wind."

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: It sounds like a compliment, but I fear that when he called Xifan a "great tree" it was in the sense that "the greatest tree in a forest is the first to be crushed by the wind."

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Of course. Those two often butted heads, but one must always be careful when penning words down. Words penned in black and white can hardly be taken back, after all.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: In response, Xifan penned the following: "Spring will come, and the tree shall yield lush shade."

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: And here, too. I remember that the one who wrote this was Tianquan at some point. They say that he was brilliant at both calligraphy and swordplay, but that his comments were always very concise.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: This is what he wrote: "Lovely, but you never did learn how to sign your name."

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: There's all sorts of other interesting annotations too. Come on, let me show you.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Oh, there's no rush, no rush at all. As my great-grandfather always says, to practice calligraphy is to temper heart and mind. Only by understanding this text can you learn to write the words within.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: ...Actually, wait. Do you know what time it is right now?

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Well, just look at the sky...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Oh, drat! I'm going to be late back. Looks like I'll be getting an earful from my father now!

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: *sigh* Either way, I've got to go face the music now. I'll be back later to practice my swordplay again, though, so if you have time, why not come and join me?

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: I'm sure that we'll improve all the faster by putting our heads together and putting one another to the test.

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: But if you don't want to practice, we can always take a walk, or even go fishing...

response.speaker: Xingqiu
response.text: Heh. Look at me, rambling on like this... I'll head back first. See you later.

choices.text: Wasn't the point to use swordplay as a way to transition to calligraphy practice?
Quite the backhanded compliment, you can barely tell it's criticism...
